source: Scene-locked vertical (Instagram) POSITIVE-CASE reel for the Resurrection tab (ev-s2), ported from the certified library/emptytomb.html (re-certified 2026-09-29): the checkable claim, Joseph of Arimathea, the enemies' stolen-body polemic ('most naturally read as conceding'), the women witnesses (Josephus Ant. 4.219), the Jerusalem factor ('no source records anyone doing so'), 1 Cor 15:4, and the essay's bounded verdict ('in all probability ... found empty'; 'the most natural explanation ... rose bodily').
voiceover: Was Jesus' tomb really empty? The first Christians made a claim anyone in Jerusalem could check with a short walk: the grave was empty. All four Gospels say he was laid in the rock tomb of Joseph of Arimathea — a member of the very council that had handed him over. A named tomb, with a named owner. The earliest Jewish reply we can recover was not, the body is still there. It was, his disciples came by night and stole him — an answer most naturally read as conceding the tomb was empty. Every Gospel says women found it first — in a world where Josephus could write, let not the testimony of women be admitted. They are the last witnesses anyone inventing the story would choose. And it was proclaimed in Jerusalem itself — the one city where producing the body would have ended it. No source records anyone doing so. The early creed Paul passes on already implies it: he was buried, and he was raised on the third day. Taken together, the evidence says that in all probability, the tomb was found empty. And with the appearances, for anyone not ruling out miracles, the most natural explanation of it all is that Jesus rose bodily from the dead.
